body:
The following plasma enzyme activities are often increased when the corresponding liver disease(s) is/are present.

a. ALT and fulminant hepatitis
b. AST and Dubin-Johnson's syndrome
c. GGT and intra-hepatic cholestasis
d. Alkaline phosphatase and extrahepatic cholestasis
e. 5' nucleotidase and cholestasis secondary to drug-induced hepatitis

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. ALT and fulminant hepatitis | **T** | Massive hepatocyte necrosis releases ALT. |
| b. AST and Dubin-Johnson's syndrome | **F** | Dubin–Johnson is a benign defect of conjugated bilirubin excretion with normal enzymes. |
| c. GGT and intra-hepatic cholestasis | **T** | GGT rises in cholestasis. |
| d. Alkaline phosphatase and extrahepatic cholestasis | **T** | ALP rises markedly in obstruction. |
| e. 5' nucleotidase and cholestasis secondary to drug-induced hepatitis | **T** | 5'NT parallels hepatic ALP in cholestasis. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c T, d T, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Hepatocellular** damage raises the **aminotransferases (ALT, AST)**; **cholestasis** (intra- or extrahepatic) raises **ALP, GGT and 5'-nucleotidase**. Inherited hyperbilirubinaemias (Gilbert, Crigler–Najjar, Dubin–Johnson, Rotor) have **normal enzymes**.

## Simplified explanation

Damage → ALT/AST; blockage → ALP/GGT/5'NT; Dubin–Johnson has normal enzymes.

body:
Intrinsic (renal) causes of acute kidney injury include...

a. Acute pyelonephritis
b. Renal artery stenosis
c. Bilateral ureterolithiasis
d. Acute glomerulonephritis
e. Benign prostatic hypertrophy

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Acute pyelonephritis | **T** | Renal parenchymal infection. |
| b. Renal artery stenosis | **F** | Reduced perfusion – pre-renal. |
| c. Bilateral ureterolithiasis | **F** | Obstruction – post-renal. |
| d. Acute glomerulonephritis | **T** | Glomerular disease – intrinsic. |
| e. Benign prostatic hypertrophy | **F** | Outflow obstruction – post-renal. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c F, d T, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

AKI is classified as **pre-renal** (hypoperfusion: hypovolaemia, heart failure, renal artery stenosis), **intrinsic/renal** (acute tubular necrosis, **glomerulonephritis**, interstitial nephritis, **pyelonephritis**, vasculitis) and **post-renal** (obstruction: **stones**, **prostatic hypertrophy**/cancer, tumours).

## Simplified explanation

Kidney tissue diseases (pyelonephritis, glomerulonephritis) are intrinsic; artery stenosis is pre-renal; stones and prostate are post-renal.

body:
In relation to chronic kidney disease,...

a. There is primary hyperparathyroidism
b. Hyperphosphataemia is always present
c. There is reduced bone resorption of calcium
d. Anaemia is due mainly to the deficiency of iron
e. Vascular stiffening is due to increased Ca × P product

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. There is primary hyperparathyroidism | **F** | It is secondary (and later tertiary) hyperparathyroidism. |
| b. Hyperphosphataemia is always present | **F** | Only in advanced CKD (GFR < ~30). |
| c. There is reduced bone resorption of calcium | **F** | High PTH increases bone resorption. |
| d. Anaemia is due mainly to the deficiency of iron | **F** | Mainly erythropoietin deficiency. |
| e. Vascular stiffening is due to increased Ca × P product | **T** | A high calcium–phosphate product drives vascular calcification. |

> [!answer]
> a F, b F, c F, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In CKD, phosphate retention and reduced **1α-hydroxylation** of vitamin D lower calcium and stimulate **secondary hyperparathyroidism**, increasing **bone resorption** (renal osteodystrophy). **Hyperphosphataemia** appears in later stages. Anaemia is chiefly due to **erythropoietin deficiency**. A raised **Ca × PO₄ product** causes **vascular calcification and stiffening**.

## Simplified explanation

CKD gives secondary (not primary) hyperparathyroidism, EPO-deficient anaemia and vessel calcification from a high Ca×P product.

body:
Consider the following statements about the use of glycated compounds in the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus.

a. They are useful in the monitoring of type 2 diabetes mellitus
b. They cannot be used in monitoring secondary diabetes mellitus
c. HbA1c is useful for short-term monitoring of type 2 diabetes mellitus
d. Glycated compounds are best for diagnosis of secondary diabetes mellitus
e. Fructosamine is only useful in monitoring of type 1 diabetes mellitus in adults

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. They are useful in the monitoring of type 2 diabetes mellitus | **T** | HbA1c and fructosamine monitor glycaemic control. |
| b. They cannot be used in monitoring secondary diabetes mellitus | **F** | They reflect glycaemia whatever the cause. |
| c. HbA1c is useful for short-term monitoring of type 2 diabetes mellitus | **F** | HbA1c reflects the previous 2–3 months (long term). |
| d. Glycated compounds are best for diagnosis of secondary diabetes mellitus | **F** | Diagnosis of the cause needs other tests. |
| e. Fructosamine is only useful in monitoring of type 1 diabetes mellitus in adults | **F** | Useful in any diabetes, especially short-term (2–3 weeks) or when HbA1c is unreliable. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c F, d F, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**HbA1c** (glycated haemoglobin) reflects mean glycaemia over **8–12 weeks** (red cell lifespan); **fructosamine** (glycated serum proteins, mainly albumin) reflects **2–3 weeks**. Both monitor any form of diabetes; HbA1c ≥ 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) is also a diagnostic criterion.

## Simplified explanation

Glycated proteins monitor all diabetes; HbA1c is long-term, fructosamine short-term.

body:
Parathyroid hormone has the following effects:

a. Increase renal phosphate secretion
b. Increase bone resorption of calcium
c. Increase GIT absorption of vitamin D
d. Decrease renal tubular phosphate excretion
e. Decrease the formation of 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (DHCC)

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Increase renal phosphate secretion | **T** | PTH is phosphaturic. |
| b. Increase bone resorption of calcium | **T** | Via osteoclast activation (RANKL). |
| c. Increase GIT absorption of vitamin D | **F** | PTH increases renal 1α-hydroxylation of vitamin D, which raises gut calcium absorption. |
| d. Decrease renal tubular phosphate excretion | **F** | It increases phosphate excretion. |
| e. Decrease the formation of 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (DHCC) | **T** | PTH favours 1α-hydroxylation over 24-hydroxylation. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c F, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

PTH raises plasma calcium by: **bone resorption**; increased **renal calcium reabsorption**; **phosphaturia** (inhibits proximal phosphate reabsorption); and stimulation of renal **1α-hydroxylase** (more 1,25-DHCC, less 24,25-DHCC), which increases intestinal calcium absorption.

## Simplified explanation

PTH frees calcium from bone, makes the kidney lose phosphate and activate vitamin D.

body:
The following are causes of hypocalcaemia:

a. Rickets
b. Immobilisation
c. Hypervitaminosis (D)
d. Hypomagnesaemia
e. Milk-alkali syndrome

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Rickets | **T** | Vitamin D deficiency lowers calcium (and phosphate). |
| b. Immobilisation | **F** | Causes hypercalcaemia (bone resorption). |
| c. Hypervitaminosis (D) | **F** | Causes hypercalcaemia. |
| d. Hypomagnesaemia | **T** | Impairs PTH secretion and action. |
| e. Milk-alkali syndrome | **F** | Causes hypercalcaemia. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c F, d T, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Causes of **hypocalcaemia**: vitamin D deficiency (**rickets**/osteomalacia), CKD, hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism, **hypomagnesaemia**, acute pancreatitis, hyperphosphataemia. **Immobilisation, vitamin D excess and milk-alkali syndrome** cause hypercalcaemia.

## Simplified explanation

Rickets and low magnesium lower calcium; the others raise it.

body:
The following drug(s) is/are useful in the management of gout.

a. Isoniazid
b. Probenecid
c. Allopurinol
d. Ethambutol
e. Colchicine

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Isoniazid | **F** | Anti-TB drug. |
| b. Probenecid | **T** | Uricosuric. |
| c. Allopurinol | **T** | Xanthine oxidase inhibitor. |
| d. Ethambutol | **F** | Anti-TB drug that can raise urate. |
| e. Colchicine | **T** | Treats acute attacks (inhibits neutrophil microtubules). |

> [!answer]
> a F, b T, c T, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Gout treatment: acute attacks – NSAIDs, **colchicine**, corticosteroids; long-term urate lowering – **allopurinol**/febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors) and uricosurics (**probenecid**, sulfinpyrazone). Ethambutol and pyrazinamide raise urate.

## Simplified explanation

Probenecid, allopurinol and colchicine treat gout; the TB drugs do not.

body:
Consider the following statement(s) on Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

a. It is an X-linked inherited disease
b. It leads to hyperuricaemia and hyperuricosuria
c. The condition results from deficiency of 5'-PRPP
d. In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome the enzyme APRT is deficient
e. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome could result in megaloblastic anaemia

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. It is an X-linked inherited disease | **T** | X-linked recessive. |
| b. It leads to hyperuricaemia and hyperuricosuria | **T** | Purine overproduction. |
| c. The condition results from deficiency of 5'-PRPP | **F** | PRPP accumulates; the deficient enzyme is HGPRT. |
| d. In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome the enzyme APRT is deficient | **F** | HGPRT (HPRT) is deficient; APRT deficiency causes 2,8-dihydroxyadenine stones. |
| e. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome could result in megaloblastic anaemia | **T** | A recognised feature. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c F, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Lesch–Nyhan syndrome** is X-linked complete deficiency of **hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT)**, the salvage enzyme. Unused hypoxanthine/guanine and accumulated **PRPP** drive de novo purine synthesis → **hyperuricaemia, uricosuria**, gout, stones, plus self-mutilation, dystonia and intellectual disability; megaloblastic anaemia can occur.

## Simplified explanation

X-linked HGPRT deficiency → too much uric acid; PRPP builds up.

body:
Increased AST/ALT activity in liver disease suggests the following causes.

a. Infective agents
b. Autoimmune disorders
c. Paracetamol overdose
d. Poisonous mushroom (Amanita phalloides)
e. Viral hepatitis if the AST/ALT is greater than 2.5

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Infective agents | **T** | Viral hepatitis etc. |
| b. Autoimmune disorders | **T** | Autoimmune hepatitis. |
| c. Paracetamol overdose | **T** | Very high transaminases. |
| d. Poisonous mushroom (Amanita phalloides) | **T** | Severe hepatocellular necrosis. |
| e. Viral hepatitis if the AST/ALT is greater than 2.5 | **F** | AST/ALT > 2 suggests alcoholic liver disease; viral hepatitis usually < 1. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c T, d T, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Raised transaminases indicate **hepatocellular injury**: viruses, autoimmune hepatitis, drugs/toxins (paracetamol, Amanita), ischaemia, alcohol, Wilson's disease. The **AST:ALT (de Ritis) ratio** is usually **< 1** in viral hepatitis and **> 2** in alcoholic liver disease.

## Simplified explanation

All are causes of high AST/ALT, but a ratio > 2 points to alcohol, not viral hepatitis.

body:
The following plasma enzyme activities are often increased when the corresponding forms of liver disease are present:

a. ALT and Gilbert's syndrome
b. Caeruloplasmin and hepatolenticular degeneration (Wilson's disease)
c. AST and acute viral hepatitis
d. Alkaline phosphatase and extrahepatic cholestasis
e. GGT and intrahepatic cholestasis

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. ALT and Gilbert's syndrome | **F** | Gilbert's has normal enzymes. |
| b. Caeruloplasmin and hepatolenticular degeneration (Wilson's disease) | **F** | Caeruloplasmin is usually low in Wilson's disease. |
| c. AST and acute viral hepatitis | **T** | Hepatocellular injury. |
| d. Alkaline phosphatase and extrahepatic cholestasis | **T** | Obstruction. |
| e. GGT and intrahepatic cholestasis | **T** | Cholestasis. |

> [!answer]
> a F, b F, c T, d T, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Gilbert's syndrome is an isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with **normal enzymes**. In **Wilson's disease**, plasma **caeruloplasmin is reduced**. Transaminases rise in viral hepatitis; ALP and GGT in cholestasis.

## Simplified explanation

Gilbert's: normal enzymes; Wilson's: low caeruloplasmin.

body:
In the diagnosis of acute hepatitis the following biochemical picture is observed.

a. [ALT] is always twice the [AST]
b. [AST] is always twice the [ALT]
c. [Albumin] is decreased or unchanged
d. [Albumin] is increased or unchanged
e. de Ritis ratio is > 1

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. [ALT] is always twice the [AST] | **F** | ALT usually exceeds AST, but not 'always twice'. |
| b. [AST] is always twice the [ALT] | **F** | That pattern suggests alcoholic liver disease. |
| c. [Albumin] is decreased or unchanged | **T** | Albumin is usually normal (long half-life) or slightly low. |
| d. [Albumin] is increased or unchanged | **F** | Albumin does not rise. |
| e. de Ritis ratio is > 1 | **F** | AST/ALT is usually < 1 in acute viral hepatitis. |

> [!answer]
> a F, b F, c T, d F, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In acute (viral) hepatitis transaminases rise markedly (often > 10× normal) with **ALT > AST** (de Ritis ratio **< 1**). **Albumin** (half-life ~20 days) is usually **normal or slightly reduced**. 'Always' statements are false.

## Simplified explanation

Acute hepatitis: ALT higher than AST, albumin normal or low.

body:
Which of the following conditions is a post-renal cause of acute renal failure?

a. Acute glomerulonephritis
b. Renal artery stenosis
c. Prostate cancer
d. Benign prostatic hypertrophy
e. Chronic hypertension

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Acute glomerulonephritis | **F** | Intrinsic. |
| b. Renal artery stenosis | **F** | Pre-renal. |
| c. Prostate cancer | **T** | Outflow obstruction. |
| d. Benign prostatic hypertrophy | **T** | Outflow obstruction. |
| e. Chronic hypertension | **F** | Causes chronic kidney disease. |

> [!answer]
> a F, b F, c T, d T, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Post-renal** failure results from **urinary tract obstruction** – prostatic enlargement (BPH, carcinoma), stones, tumours, strictures.

## Simplified explanation

Prostate problems block urine flow: post-renal.

body:
The biochemical picture in osteoporosis includes...

a. Reduced calcium
b. Normal calcium
c. Reduced phosphate
d. Increased phosphate
e. Normal alkaline phosphatase

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Reduced calcium | **F** | Calcium is normal. |
| b. Normal calcium | **T** | Typical. |
| c. Reduced phosphate | **F** | Normal. |
| d. Increased phosphate | **F** | Normal. |
| e. Normal alkaline phosphatase | **T** | Normal (unless recent fracture). |

> [!answer]
> a F, b T, c F, d F, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **osteoporosis** (reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation), serum **calcium, phosphate and ALP are normal**. Abnormal results suggest another bone disease (osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism, Paget's, malignancy).

## Simplified explanation

Osteoporosis: normal calcium, phosphate and ALP.

body:
Consider the following statements on calcitonin and calcitriol:

a. Calcitonin is secreted in response to low levels of plasma calcium
b. Calcitriol is derived from vitamin D by hydroxylation in the liver only
c. Calcitriol is derived from vitamin D3 by hydroxylation in the kidney only
d. Calcitriol is derived from hydroxylation of vitamin D in the liver and the kidney
e. Calcitonin and calcitriol have contrasting functions

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Calcitonin is secreted in response to low levels of plasma calcium | **F** | It is secreted when calcium is high. |
| b. Calcitriol is derived from vitamin D by hydroxylation in the liver only | **F** | Liver (25-) then kidney (1α-). |
| c. Calcitriol is derived from vitamin D3 by hydroxylation in the kidney only | **F** | Needs liver 25-hydroxylation first. |
| d. Calcitriol is derived from hydroxylation of vitamin D in the liver and the kidney | **T** | 25-hydroxylation (liver) then 1α-hydroxylation (kidney). |
| e. Calcitonin and calcitriol have contrasting functions | **T** | Calcitonin lowers calcium; calcitriol raises it. |

> [!answer]
> a F, b F, c F, d T, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Calcitonin** (thyroid C cells) is released in **hypercalcaemia** and inhibits osteoclasts. **Calcitriol** (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) is formed by **25-hydroxylation in the liver** then **1α-hydroxylation in the kidney**; it raises calcium (gut absorption, bone mobilisation).

## Simplified explanation

Calcitonin lowers calcium; calcitriol (made in liver then kidney) raises it.

body:
Consider the following statements on hyperuricaemia and gout:

a. Hyperuricaemia can be primary or secondary
b. Gout will never occur in persons with normal uric acid levels
c. Temperature is a key determinant in the pathogenesis of gout
d. Teetotallers are at an increased risk of developing gout
e. Antihypertensive agents reduce one's risk of uric acid retention

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Hyperuricaemia can be primary or secondary | **T** | Primary (idiopathic/enzyme defects) or secondary (other diseases/drugs). |
| b. Gout will never occur in persons with normal uric acid levels | **F** | Acute gout can occur with a normal urate during the attack. |
| c. Temperature is a key determinant in the pathogenesis of gout | **T** | Urate is less soluble at lower temperatures (peripheral joints). |
| d. Teetotallers are at an increased risk of developing gout | **F** | Alcohol increases risk. |
| e. Antihypertensive agents reduce one's risk of uric acid retention | **F** | Thiazide and loop diuretics increase urate retention. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c T, d F, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Gout results from deposition of **monosodium urate** crystals. Solubility falls at **lower temperature** and pH, explaining predilection for the big toe. Serum urate can be normal during an acute attack. Alcohol, purine-rich diet, obesity and **diuretics** raise urate.

## Simplified explanation

Hyperuricaemia is primary or secondary; cold joints favour crystals; alcohol and diuretics raise urate.

body:
A man aged 35 years, with a five-year history of ankylosing spondylitis, presented with a ten-day history of anorexia, malaise, loss of weight and mild diffuse right upper abdominal pain. Five days previously he noticed that his urine was dark, and three days before admission his wife noticed that he was becoming increasingly yellow. He had been treated with indomethacin for his spinal condition, but this had recently been changed to **phenylbutazone**. He had no contact with infectious hepatitis patients, no recent intravenous therapy or blood transfusion, and was a teetotaller. On examination he was jaundiced with a tender liver 3 cm below the costal margin; no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

| Plasma | Result |
|---|---|
| Total protein | 71 g/L (60–80) |
| Albumin | 39 g/L (30–50) |
| Alkaline phosphatase | 585 IU/L (<120) |
| ALT | 536 IU/L (<35) |
| Direct bilirubin | 72 µmol/L (<6.5) |
| Total bilirubin | 120 µmol/L (<20) |

Urine: bilirubin positive; urobilinogen increased.

i. What is the diagnosis? *(2)*  ii. What is the cause of the patient's condition? *(2)*  iii. Explain the cause stated in (ii). *(4)*  iv. Suggest two other biochemical tests. *(2)*
answer:
**i.** **Acute (drug-induced) hepatitis with a mixed hepatocellular–cholestatic picture** – acute hepatocellular jaundice: very high ALT (~15× ULN), raised ALP (~5×), conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with bilirubinuria; albumin and total protein normal (acute, not chronic).

**ii.** **Drug-induced liver injury due to phenylbutazone** (idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity); viral, alcoholic and transfusion causes are unlikely from the history.

**iii.** Phenylbutazone (an NSAID) is metabolised in the liver to reactive metabolites that cause **idiosyncratic hypersensitivity/metabolic injury** to hepatocytes: hepatocyte necrosis releases **ALT**, and damage to the canalicular excretory apparatus causes **intrahepatic cholestasis** (raised ALP, **conjugated** bilirubin that spills into urine). Impaired hepatic uptake of urobilinogen reabsorbed from the gut raises urinary **urobilinogen**. The temporal link with starting the drug supports the cause.

**iv.** Any two: **GGT** (confirms hepatic origin of ALP), **AST**, **prothrombin time/INR** (synthetic function, severity), **viral hepatitis serology** (HAV IgM, HBsAg, anti-HCV) to exclude viral causes, serum bile acids, repeat LFTs after stopping the drug.

> [!answer]
> Acute drug-induced (phenylbutazone) hepatitis with cholestatic component; confirm with GGT, PT/INR and viral serology.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Acute hepatocellular injury gives transaminases > 10× ULN with smaller ALP rises; cholestasis gives ALP > 3× with smaller transaminase rises. Here both are high – a **mixed** picture typical of drug-induced hepatitis. A normal albumin indicates an acute process.

## Simplified explanation

The new drug (phenylbutazone) has injured his liver: very high ALT and raised ALP with conjugated bilirubin in the urine.

body:
BB, a 47-year-old fishmonger, was admitted following an episode of haematemesis. Endoscopy revealed oesophageal varices. The only biochemical abnormality was an elevated GGT (245 IU/L). The varices were treated by sclerotherapy and she was told to abstain from alcohol. She was readmitted later with jaundice, drowsiness and other signs of clinical liver disease:

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Albumin | 25 g/L |
| Bilirubin | 260 µmol/L |
| Alkaline phosphatase | 315 IU/L |
| ALT | 134 IU/L |
| AST | 167 IU/L |
| GGT | 360 IU/L |

If BB had a prolonged prothrombin time:
i. Give a diagnosis for BB's condition. *(2)*  ii. Explain your diagnosis. *(3)*  iii. Suggest two other tests to the clinician. *(2)*  iv. Justify your suggestion. *(3)*
answer:
**i.** **Decompensated alcoholic liver cirrhosis** (chronic liver failure) with portal hypertension and **hepatic encephalopathy**.

**ii.** Oesophageal varices indicate **portal hypertension**; isolated high GGT initially reflects **alcohol** enzyme induction. Later: **low albumin** and **prolonged PT** show failing **synthetic function**; very high bilirubin with jaundice shows failing excretion; **AST > ALT** (de Ritis ratio > 1) and very high GGT are typical of **alcoholic** liver disease; drowsiness suggests **encephalopathy** from hyperammonaemia.

**iii and iv.** Any two, justified:
- **Plasma ammonia** – supports hepatic encephalopathy as the cause of drowsiness.
- **Blood glucose** – hypoglycaemia from failed gluconeogenesis can cause drowsiness.
- **Urea, creatinine and electrolytes** – detect hepatorenal syndrome, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia.
- **Serum protein electrophoresis/immunoglobulins** – polyclonal increase and β–γ bridging in cirrhosis.
- **Viral serology (HBsAg, anti-HCV), ferritin/iron studies, α-fetoprotein** – exclude other causes and hepatocellular carcinoma.
- **Full blood count** – macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism).

> [!answer]
> Decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis with encephalopathy; suggest ammonia and glucose (or U&E, AFP, viral markers) to explain drowsiness and complications.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Albumin and clotting factors measure **synthetic function**; their failure with jaundice and encephalopathy indicates **decompensated cirrhosis**. The alcoholic pattern is AST > ALT with markedly raised GGT.

## Simplified explanation

She has alcohol-related cirrhosis that has failed: varices, low albumin, long clotting time, jaundice and confusion.

body:
Madam AK, a retired midwife who lived alone, was admitted after her son found her semi-conscious in her apartment. A week earlier she had been well. On examination she was severely dehydrated but **not ketotic**; her respiration was normal.

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Na | 149 mmol/L (132–142) |
| K | 4.7 mmol/L (3.5–4.9) |
| HCO₃⁻ | 18 mmol/L (24–28) |
| Urea | 35 mmol/L (2.1–7.2) |
| Creatinine | 180 µmol/L (50–110) |
| Glucose | 54 mmol/L (3.4–6.1) |
| Total protein | 90 g/L (60–80) |
| Osmolality | 370 mOsm/kg (285–310) |

i. Comment on Madam AK's results.  ii. What is the reason for her high urea and creatinine levels?  iii. What is her diagnosis?  iv. What further test(s) will you suggest?
answer:
**i.** Marked **hyperglycaemia** (54 mmol/L) with very high **osmolality** (370; calculated ≈ 2(149 + 4.7) + 54 + 35 ≈ 396), **hypernatraemia**, high **total protein** (haemoconcentration), raised **urea** disproportionate to **creatinine**, normal potassium and only a **mild fall in bicarbonate** without ketosis or Kussmaul breathing.

**ii.** **Pre-renal uraemia** from severe **dehydration**: osmotic diuresis from glycosuria causes water and salt loss → reduced renal perfusion and GFR; urea rises more than creatinine because of increased tubular urea reabsorption at low flow.

**iii.** **Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS; hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma)**, probably in previously undiagnosed **type 2 diabetes**.

**iv.** **Urine/blood ketones** (β-hydroxybutyrate) to confirm absence of ketoacidosis; **arterial blood gas and anion gap/lactate**; repeat **electrolytes, glucose and osmolality** during treatment; **HbA1c**; screen for precipitant – **infection** (FBC, CRP, blood/urine culture, chest X-ray), cardiac enzymes/ECG (MI), and a coagulation screen given high thrombotic risk.

> [!answer]
> Severe hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality, hypernatraemia and pre-renal uraemia without ketosis → HHS (hyperosmolar non-ketotic state); check ketones, gases, HbA1c and look for infection.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In HHS, enough insulin remains to suppress ketogenesis but not hyperglycaemia; profound **osmotic diuresis** causes dehydration, hyperosmolality and pre-renal uraemia. It typically affects elderly patients with type 2 diabetes and carries a high mortality and thrombosis risk.

## Simplified explanation

Very high sugar and salt-concentrated blood from dehydration, without ketones: hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.

body: List **three** endocrine causes of secondary diabetes and explain the mechanism in each case. *(6 marks)*
answer:
| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Cushing's syndrome** (glucocorticoid excess) | Cortisol stimulates gluconeogenesis and causes insulin resistance |
| **Acromegaly** (growth hormone excess) | GH antagonises insulin action (insulin resistance) and increases hepatic glucose output |
| **Phaeochromocytoma** (catecholamine excess) | Adrenaline inhibits insulin secretion and stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis |
| **Thyrotoxicosis** | Increased gut glucose absorption and hepatic glucose output |
| **Glucagonoma** | Glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis |
| **Conn's syndrome** | Hypokalaemia impairs insulin secretion |

> [!answer]
> Any three, e.g. Cushing's (cortisol → gluconeogenesis, insulin resistance), acromegaly (GH → insulin resistance), phaeochromocytoma (catecholamines → reduced insulin, more glycogenolysis).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hormones that **oppose insulin** (cortisol, GH, catecholamines, glucagon, thyroid hormone) cause secondary diabetes when produced in excess, by increasing hepatic glucose output, inducing insulin resistance or suppressing insulin secretion.

## Simplified explanation

Too much cortisol, growth hormone or adrenaline works against insulin and raises blood sugar.

body:
i. What is **fructosamine** and why would you estimate it in a diabetic patient? *(2 marks)*

ii. Explain why fructosamine may be preferred over glycated haemoglobin in medical laboratory practice. *(3 marks)*
answer:
**i.** Fructosamine is the collective name for **glycated serum proteins** (mainly **albumin**) formed by non-enzymatic glycation (ketoamine). Because albumin's half-life is ~20 days, it reflects **average glycaemia over the previous 2–3 weeks**, so it is used to monitor **short-term control** (e.g. after a change of treatment, in pregnancy).

**ii.** Fructosamine is preferred when **HbA1c is unreliable**: haemoglobin variants (HbS, HbC common in Ghana), haemolytic anaemia, blood loss or transfusion, iron deficiency and altered red cell lifespan; it gives **faster feedback** (2–3 weeks), and is a **cheap, simple colorimetric assay** easily automated on routine chemistry analysers. (It is unreliable when albumin is abnormal, e.g. nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis.)

> [!answer]
> Glycated serum (albumin) protein reflecting 2–3 weeks' glycaemia; useful when HbA1c is unreliable (Hb variants, haemolysis, transfusion), gives faster feedback and is cheap/automated.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

HbA1c depends on red cell lifespan (~120 days) and haemoglobin structure; fructosamine depends on serum protein turnover. Each is chosen according to the clinical question and confounders.

## Simplified explanation

Fructosamine is glycated albumin showing the last 2–3 weeks of sugar control; it's useful when HbA1c can't be trusted.

body: Give **two** reasons for the chronic anaemia observed in a patient with chronic kidney disease.
answer:
1. **Erythropoietin deficiency** – damaged peritubular interstitial cells produce less EPO (main cause).
2. **Shortened red cell survival** from uraemic toxins.
3. **Iron deficiency/functional iron deficiency** (blood loss, raised hepcidin from inflammation).
4. **Uraemic bone-marrow suppression**, blood loss (dialysis, GI bleeding, platelet dysfunction), folate deficiency, hyperparathyroidism (marrow fibrosis).

> [!answer]
> EPO deficiency and reduced red cell survival (also iron deficiency/blood loss, marrow suppression).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

CKD anaemia is normochromic normocytic and mainly due to **reduced EPO**; it responds to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents once iron stores are replete.

## Simplified explanation

Diseased kidneys make little EPO, and uraemia shortens red cell life.

body: Explain the cause of the frequent **hyperuricaemia** in Kofi Brokeman, the alcoholic in the locality.
answer:
Alcohol raises urate by:
- **Increased production**: ethanol metabolism accelerates **ATP breakdown** to AMP → adenosine → inosine → hypoxanthine → xanthine → **uric acid**; beer also contains **purines** (guanosine).
- **Reduced excretion**: ethanol metabolism produces **lactate** (raised NADH/NAD⁺) and ketoacids, which **compete with urate for renal tubular secretion**; dehydration further reduces excretion.

> [!answer]
> Increased ATP turnover/purine load raises urate production, and lactate (and ketones) from ethanol metabolism inhibit renal urate excretion.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hyperuricaemia results from **overproduction** (high purine turnover) or **underexcretion** (renal). Alcohol does both.

## Simplified explanation

Alcohol makes more uric acid and the lactate it produces stops the kidney getting rid of it.

body: Explain why a patient with chronic kidney disease will develop **renal osteodystrophy**.
answer:
1. **Phosphate retention** (reduced GFR) → hyperphosphataemia, which lowers ionised calcium and directly stimulates PTH and **FGF-23**.
2. **Reduced renal 1α-hydroxylase** (loss of renal mass, inhibited by FGF-23 and phosphate) → **low calcitriol** → poor gut calcium absorption → **hypocalcaemia** and defective mineralisation (osteomalacia).
3. Low calcium, high phosphate and low calcitriol → **secondary hyperparathyroidism** → increased osteoclastic **bone resorption** (osteitis fibrosa cystica); later autonomous (tertiary) hyperparathyroidism.
4. **Metabolic acidosis** – bone buffers acid, releasing calcium carbonate.
5. Others: aluminium accumulation (adynamic bone), β2-microglobulin amyloid in dialysis.

> [!answer]
> Phosphate retention + reduced calcitriol → hypocalcaemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism with bone resorption, plus defective mineralisation and acidosis.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Renal osteodystrophy** (CKD–mineral and bone disorder) encompasses osteitis fibrosa, osteomalacia, adynamic bone and mixed disease, with vascular calcification from a high Ca × P product.

## Simplified explanation

Damaged kidneys keep phosphate and stop activating vitamin D, so calcium falls, PTH rises and bone is broken down.

body: What will be the levels (HIGH, LOW or NORMAL) of the following in a patient with **secondary hyperparathyroidism** (due to chronic kidney disease)? i. Calcium ii. Phosphate iii. Calcitriol iv. Magnesium. v. What reason(s) would you assign for the observed calcitriol levels?
answer:
| Analyte | Level |
|---|---|
| Calcium | **Low** (or low-normal) |
| Phosphate | **High** |
| Calcitriol | **Low** |
| Magnesium | **High** (reduced renal excretion) |

**v.** Calcitriol is low because **diseased kidneys have less 1α-hydroxylase**, and **hyperphosphataemia and FGF-23 inhibit** 1α-hydroxylation.

> [!answer]
> Ca low, PO₄ high, calcitriol low, Mg high; low calcitriol from loss of renal 1α-hydroxylase and inhibition by phosphate/FGF-23.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Secondary hyperparathyroidism is an appropriate PTH response to **hypocalcaemia**, most often from CKD or vitamin D deficiency. In vitamin D deficiency, phosphate is low rather than high.

## Simplified explanation

In CKD: calcium low, phosphate high, active vitamin D low, magnesium high.

body: Explain how a person with **von Gierke's disease** will develop hyperuricaemia.
answer:
In von Gierke's disease (**glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency**, GSD type Ia):
- **Increased production**: G6P accumulates and is shunted into the **pentose phosphate pathway**, raising ribose-5-phosphate and **PRPP**, which drives **de novo purine synthesis**; fasting hypoglycaemia lowers hepatic phosphate/ATP, increasing **AMP degradation** to uric acid.
- **Reduced excretion**: excess G6P goes to **lactate** (lactic acidosis), and lactate **competes with urate** for renal tubular secretion.

> [!answer]
> More purine synthesis (G6P → PRPP) and ATP breakdown, plus lactate inhibiting renal urate excretion.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hyperuricaemia, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidaemia and fasting hypoglycaemia are the metabolic hallmarks of von Gierke's disease.

## Simplified explanation

Excess glucose-6-phosphate makes more purines, and lactate blocks urate excretion.

body: Distinguish between **primary** and **tertiary** hyperparathyroidism (state one cause each).
answer:
**Primary hyperparathyroidism** – autonomous excess PTH from the parathyroid gland itself, with **high calcium** and low phosphate. Cause: **parathyroid adenoma** (~85%), hyperplasia, carcinoma, MEN 1/2A.

**Tertiary hyperparathyroidism** – **autonomous** PTH secretion developing after long-standing **secondary** hyperparathyroidism; glands become hyperplastic/nodular and no longer respond to calcium, giving **hypercalcaemia**. Cause: long-standing **chronic kidney disease** (often noticed after renal transplantation).

> [!answer]
> Primary: gland disease (adenoma) causing hypercalcaemia. Tertiary: autonomous glands after prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism (CKD).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Secondary hyperparathyroidism is an appropriate response to low calcium; when it persists, glands become autonomous (tertiary).

## Simplified explanation

Primary = a faulty gland (adenoma). Tertiary = glands that went rogue after years of kidney disease.
hint: Where does the drive come from?

body: What is **reactive hypoglycaemia**? What conditions must be satisfied in order to diagnose hypoglycaemia?
answer:
**Reactive (postprandial) hypoglycaemia** is hypoglycaemia occurring **2–5 hours after a meal** (especially carbohydrate-rich), due to an exaggerated or mistimed insulin response (e.g. after gastric surgery – late dumping, early type 2 diabetes).

**Diagnosis – Whipple's triad:**
1. **Symptoms** consistent with hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, palpitations, confusion).
2. **Low plasma glucose** measured at the time of symptoms (typically < 2.8–3.0 mmol/L in adults).
3. **Relief of symptoms** when glucose is raised.

> [!answer]
> Hypoglycaemia a few hours after meals from excess insulin response; diagnosis requires Whipple's triad.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hypoglycaemia must be **biochemically confirmed** with appropriate symptoms; glucose samples need a fluoride tube to prevent in-vitro glycolysis.

## Simplified explanation

Low sugar after eating; diagnosed when symptoms, a low glucose reading and relief with sugar all occur.

body: Explain why you will choose **creatinine** over **urea** as a measure of clearance in the assessment of kidney function.
answer:
- Creatinine is produced at a **fairly constant rate** from muscle creatine; urea production varies with **dietary protein, catabolism, GI bleeding, liver function**.
- Creatinine is **freely filtered** and **not reabsorbed** (only slightly secreted), so its clearance approximates GFR; urea is **passively reabsorbed** (40–50%, more at low urine flow/dehydration), so urea clearance underestimates GFR.
- Creatinine is less affected by **hydration status**.

> [!answer]
> Creatinine production is steady and it is not reabsorbed, so its clearance approximates GFR; urea varies with diet/catabolism and is reabsorbed.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

An ideal GFR marker is produced at a constant rate, freely filtered, and neither reabsorbed nor secreted (inulin, iohexol). Creatinine comes closer than urea.

## Simplified explanation

Creatinine is made steadily and not reabsorbed, so it reflects GFR better than urea.

body: What is the **salvage pathway**? What is its role in the de novo synthesis of uric acid?
answer:
The **purine salvage pathway** recycles free purine bases (hypoxanthine, guanine, adenine) back to nucleotides using **PRPP**, catalysed by **HGPRT** (hypoxanthine, guanine → IMP, GMP) and **APRT** (adenine → AMP).

**Role:** it conserves purines and **consumes PRPP**, and the nucleotides formed **feedback-inhibit** PRPP amidotransferase (the first committed enzyme of de novo synthesis). It therefore **limits de novo purine synthesis and uric acid formation**. If salvage fails (HGPRT deficiency – Lesch–Nyhan, Kelley–Seegmiller), bases are degraded to **uric acid**, PRPP accumulates and de novo synthesis increases → hyperuricaemia.

> [!answer]
> Recycling of purine bases to nucleotides by HGPRT/APRT; it uses PRPP and feedback-inhibits de novo synthesis, so reducing uric acid production.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Most purines are recycled; only a fraction is degraded to urate. Salvage defects therefore cause purine overproduction.

## Simplified explanation

The salvage pathway recycles purine bases so fewer new purines (and less uric acid) are made.

body: Distinguish between **overflow proteinuria** and **orthostatic proteinuria**.
answer:
**Overflow proteinuria** – the glomerulus is normal but the plasma contains excess **low-molecular-weight proteins** that are filtered beyond the tubular reabsorptive capacity: e.g. **Bence Jones protein** (free light chains) in myeloma, **myoglobin** (rhabdomyolysis), **haemoglobin** (intravascular haemolysis), lysozyme.

**Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria** – a benign condition, usually in adolescents/young adults, in which protein appears in urine collected while **upright** but is **absent in an early-morning (recumbent) sample**; total usually < 1 g/day.

> [!answer]
> Overflow = excess small plasma proteins exceed tubular reabsorption (Bence Jones, myoglobin); orthostatic = benign posture-related proteinuria absent on lying down.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Proteinuria is classified as glomerular, tubular, overflow, and post-renal; orthostatic proteinuria is diagnosed by comparing split (recumbent vs upright) collections.

## Simplified explanation

Overflow: too much small protein in blood spills into urine. Orthostatic: protein only when standing, harmless.

body: Briefly explain why a patient with **end-stage kidney disease** and **liver failure** will develop hypoglycaemia.
answer:
- **Liver failure**: loss of hepatic **glycogen stores** and impaired **gluconeogenesis** and glycogenolysis; reduced insulin degradation by the liver.
- **End-stage kidney disease**: the kidney is a site of **gluconeogenesis** (~20–40% in fasting) and of **insulin clearance**; reduced renal mass lowers glucose production and prolongs insulin (and sulphonylurea) action; poor nutrition.

> [!answer]
> Reduced hepatic and renal gluconeogenesis and glycogen stores, with reduced clearance of insulin.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Glucose homeostasis in fasting depends on hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (liver and kidney). Failure of both organs removes these sources and prolongs insulin action.

## Simplified explanation

Both the liver and kidney make glucose and remove insulin; when they fail, sugar drops.
hint: Both organs make glucose and clear insulin.

body: Give the significance of the following: a. ALT/AST ratio in the diagnosis of liver disease; b. fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) in the investigation of kidney disease; c. ALT/ALP ratio in the investigation of liver disease; d. blood urea nitrogen/creatinine (BUN/Cr) ratio in the diagnosis of kidney disease. *(8 marks)*
answer:
**a. AST:ALT (de Ritis) ratio** – < 1 (ALT > AST) is typical of acute viral and most hepatocellular injury (ALT is more liver-specific and cytosolic); **> 2** suggests **alcoholic liver disease** (mitochondrial AST, pyridoxal phosphate deficiency reduces ALT); > 1 also in cirrhosis.

**b. FENa** = (urine Na × plasma creatinine)/(plasma Na × urine creatinine) × 100. In oliguric AKI, **< 1% → pre-renal** (tubules avidly conserve sodium); **> 2% → intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis)**. Unreliable after diuretics.

**c. ALT/ALP ratio (R-value, each as multiple of ULN)** – **≥ 5 hepatocellular** injury; **≤ 2 cholestatic**; **2–5 mixed** pattern (classifies drug-induced liver injury).

**d. BUN:creatinine ratio** – normal ~10–20:1. **> 20:1 suggests pre-renal** azotaemia (increased urea reabsorption, GI bleed, catabolism; also early post-renal); **< 10–15:1 with both raised suggests intrinsic renal** damage; low ratio also in liver disease or low-protein diet.

> [!answer]
> De Ritis > 2 = alcohol, < 1 = viral; FENa < 1% pre-renal, > 2% ATN; ALT/ALP (R) ≥ 5 hepatocellular, ≤ 2 cholestatic, 2–5 mixed; BUN:Cr > 20 pre-renal, normal/low in intrinsic renal.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Ratios are more informative than single values because they reflect the **pattern** of injury (hepatocellular vs cholestatic; pre-renal vs renal), but each has confounders (diuretics, diet, liver function, muscle mass).

## Simplified explanation

Each ratio tells you which kind of liver or kidney problem it is.

body: Highlight the limitations of the following in the diagnosis of kidney disease: a. uric acid b. creatinine c. urea. *(6 marks)*
answer:
**a. Uric acid** – affected by diet (purines), alcohol, drugs (diuretics, salicylates), cell turnover (malignancy, chemotherapy), genetic overproduction; not specific for renal function.

**b. Creatinine** – depends on **muscle mass, age, sex, race** and meat intake; rises only after ~50% loss of GFR (insensitive in early disease); tubular secretion increases as GFR falls; interference (ketones, cephalosporins in Jaffe method); drugs (trimethoprim, cimetidine) block secretion.

**c. Urea** – depends on **protein intake**, **catabolism** (fever, trauma, steroids), **GI bleeding**, **liver function** (low in liver failure), **hydration** and urine flow (reabsorbed at low flow); so it is a poor index of GFR.

> [!answer]
> Uric acid – diet, drugs, cell turnover; creatinine – muscle mass/age/sex, insensitive early, secretion, interference; urea – diet, catabolism, bleeding, liver function, hydration.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Ideal kidney function markers are produced at constant rates and handled only by filtration. None of these meet this fully; eGFR equations and cystatin C partly overcome creatinine's limitations.

## Simplified explanation

Each test is affected by things other than the kidney – diet, muscle, liver, hydration.

body:
Kwame Pliers, a 48-year-old man with a twenty-year history of alcoholism, was admitted for management of alcohol withdrawal. Examination revealed slightly yellow sclera and an enlarged, hard, non-tender liver. He had been well before and was on no medication.

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Total protein | 65 g/L (60–80) |
| Albumin | 26 g/L (30–50) |
| Alkaline phosphatase | 500 U/L (30–120) |
| ALT | 70 U/L (<45) |
| Bilirubin | 45 µmol/L (<20) |
| GGT | 1180 U/L (<50) |

Give reasons for the observed levels of a. albumin b. alkaline phosphatase c. ALT. d. Suggest a diagnosis. e. Provide reasons for your answer in (d).
answer:
**a. Low albumin** – reduced hepatic **synthetic function** from chronic liver damage (cirrhosis), plus poor nutrition in alcoholism (and possibly dilution/ascites).

**b. Raised ALP (~4× ULN)** – **cholestasis**: fibrosis/regenerating nodules and swollen hepatocytes compress bile canaliculi, inducing ALP synthesis (alcohol also induces).

**c. Mildly raised ALT** – modest ongoing **hepatocellular injury**; in alcoholic disease ALT is often only mildly raised (pyridoxal phosphate deficiency; AST usually exceeds ALT).

**d.** **Alcoholic liver disease – chronic (alcoholic) cirrhosis with a cholestatic component** (alcoholic hepatitis on cirrhosis).

**e.** Long history of heavy alcohol use; **hard enlarged liver**; **markedly raised GGT** (enzyme induction by alcohol, cholestasis); **low albumin** (chronic synthetic failure); jaundice with raised ALP (cholestasis) and only mildly raised transaminases.

> [!answer]
> Low albumin – poor synthesis; high ALP – cholestasis; mild ALT – limited hepatocellular injury; diagnosis – alcoholic liver disease (cirrhosis with cholestasis), supported by very high GGT, history and hard liver.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**GGT** is induced by alcohol and rises in cholestasis; a very high GGT with raised ALP and low albumin in a heavy drinker indicates chronic alcoholic liver disease. AST:ALT > 2 would further support it.

## Simplified explanation

Years of drinking have scarred his liver: low albumin, high ALP and very high GGT.

body:
In relation to type 1 diabetes mellitus:

a. It is an autoimmune condition
b. Insulin is required for treatment
c. Type 1 diabetes mellitus in adults is called MODY
d. Both insulin and oral hypoglycaemic agents are required for treatment
e. Type 1 diabetes mellitus in a pregnant woman is called gestational diabetes

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. It is an autoimmune condition | **T** | T-cell–mediated destruction of β-cells (anti-GAD, ICA). |
| b. Insulin is required for treatment | **T** | Absolute insulin deficiency. |
| c. Type 1 diabetes mellitus in adults is called MODY | **F** | Slow autoimmune diabetes in adults is LADA; MODY is monogenic diabetes of the young. |
| d. Both insulin and oral hypoglycaemic agents are required for treatment | **F** | Insulin alone is the treatment. |
| e. Type 1 diabetes mellitus in a pregnant woman is called gestational diabetes | **F** | Gestational diabetes is diabetes first arising in pregnancy. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c F, d F, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Type 1 diabetes** results from **autoimmune** β-cell destruction, giving absolute insulin deficiency – treatment requires **insulin**. **LADA** is late-onset autoimmune diabetes in adults; **MODY** is autosomal dominant monogenic diabetes (e.g. HNF1A, glucokinase). **Gestational diabetes** is hyperglycaemia first recognised in pregnancy.

## Simplified explanation

Type 1 DM is autoimmune and needs insulin; MODY and gestational diabetes are different things.

body:
The insulin resistance syndrome or metabolic syndrome is often characterised by

a. Hyperuricaemia
b. Abdominal obesity
c. Elevated fasting HDL
d. Elevated fasting triglycerides
e. Fasting blood glucose above 5.6 mmol/L

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Hyperuricaemia | **T** | Insulin resistance reduces renal urate excretion. |
| b. Abdominal obesity | **T** | Central (visceral) obesity is a core feature. |
| c. Elevated fasting HDL | **F** | HDL is reduced. |
| d. Elevated fasting triglycerides | **T** | A defining criterion (≥ 1.7 mmol/L). |
| e. Fasting blood glucose above 5.6 mmol/L | **T** | A defining criterion. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b T, c F, d T, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Metabolic syndrome (IDF/NCEP): **central obesity**, **raised triglycerides** (≥ 1.7 mmol/L), **low HDL**, **raised blood pressure** and **fasting glucose ≥ 5.6 mmol/L**; commonly accompanied by **hyperuricaemia**, fatty liver and a prothrombotic state.

## Simplified explanation

Belly fat, high triglycerides, high glucose and high urate – but LOW HDL.

body: Give **two** reasons for the **hypocalcaemia** observed in a patient with chronic kidney disease. *(4 marks)*
answer:
1. **Reduced calcitriol**: loss of renal **1α-hydroxylase** (and inhibition by phosphate/FGF-23) lowers 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, reducing **intestinal calcium absorption**.
2. **Hyperphosphataemia**: reduced phosphate excretion; phosphate binds calcium (precipitating calcium phosphate) and lowers ionised calcium.
(3. Skeletal resistance to PTH.)

> [!answer]
> Low calcitriol (less gut Ca absorption) and phosphate retention binding calcium.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia in CKD drive secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy.

## Simplified explanation

Sick kidneys can't activate vitamin D and keep too much phosphate, so calcium falls.

body: Explain why a **serum lipid profile** is frequently requested for diabetes mellitus patients. *(4 marks)*
answer:
- Diabetes causes **dyslipidaemia**: insulin deficiency/resistance increases **lipolysis** and free fatty acid flux to the liver → increased **VLDL/triglyceride** production; reduced **lipoprotein lipase** activity slows clearance of TG-rich lipoproteins; **low HDL** and small dense LDL.
- Diabetic patients have a **high risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease**; the lipid profile assesses this risk and guides **statin/lipid-lowering therapy** and its monitoring.
- Severe hypertriglyceridaemia can cause **pancreatitis**.

> [!answer]
> Diabetes causes atherogenic dyslipidaemia (high TG/VLDL, low HDL, small dense LDL) and raises cardiovascular risk, so lipids are measured to assess risk and guide treatment.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Insulin normally activates lipoprotein lipase and suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase; lack of insulin action reverses both, causing diabetic dyslipidaemia.

## Simplified explanation

Diabetes raises bad fats and lowers good fats, increasing heart disease risk, so lipids are checked.

body: Which test(s) can be used to distinguish between hypoglycaemia due to **insulinoma** and hypoglycaemia due to an **overdose of insulin injection**? *(2 marks)*
answer:
**Plasma C-peptide** (with insulin) during hypoglycaemia:
- **Insulinoma**: high insulin **and high C-peptide** (and proinsulin) – endogenous secretion.
- **Exogenous insulin overdose**: high insulin with **suppressed/low C-peptide**, because pharmaceutical insulin contains no C-peptide.

(A sulphonylurea screen distinguishes sulphonylurea abuse, which raises both.)

> [!answer]
> C-peptide: high in insulinoma, low with injected insulin.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Endogenous insulin is secreted with **equimolar C-peptide**; injected insulin is not. Measuring both during a hypoglycaemic episode separates the causes.

## Simplified explanation

Measure **C-peptide**: high in insulinoma, low after an insulin injection overdose.
hint: Proinsulin is cleaved into insulin + C-peptide.

body: Give reason(s) for an **elevated alkaline phosphatase** level in a patient with end-stage chronic kidney disease. *(2 marks)*
answer:
**Bone (osteoblastic) ALP** rises because **secondary hyperparathyroidism** increases bone turnover (high-turnover renal osteodystrophy / osteitis fibrosa), with osteoblast activity repairing bone resorbed under PTH; defective mineralisation (osteomalacia from low calcitriol) also raises osteoblast activity.

> [!answer]
> Increased bone turnover from secondary hyperparathyroidism/renal osteodystrophy raises bone ALP.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

ALP isoenzymes come from liver and bone; in CKD the rise is usually skeletal and reflects high bone turnover.

## Simplified explanation

High PTH speeds up bone turnover, so bone ALP rises.
